$$

In this case, the $x$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(- x^{2} + 5).$ But the derivative is $- 2 x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=- x^{2} + 5.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- 2 x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad - \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\int x\left(- x^{2} + 5\right)^{4}\,\text{d}x=- \frac{1}{2}\int u^{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{2}\int u^{4}\,\text{d}u &=- \frac{1}{2}\frac{u^{5}}{5}+C\\ &=- \frac{1}{10}u^{5}+C\\ &=- \frac{\left(- x^{2} + 5\right)^{5}}{10}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the $x$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(x^{2} - 11).$ But the derivative is $2 x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=x^{2} - 11.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2 x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\int x\left(x^{2} - 11\right)^{5}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int u^{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int u^{5}\,\text{d}u &=\frac{1}{2}\frac{u^{6}}{6}+C\\ &=\frac{1}{12}u^{6}+C\\ &=\frac{\left(x^{2} - 11\right)^{6}}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
